title: Bursting and graceful-degradation strategy for enterprise POCs
content:
Summary:

This working note captures a recommended approach for enterprise POCs that need predictable baseline throughput plus occasional high-short bursts (5–30 minutes) while controlling GPU spend and preserving latency SLOs. It is aimed at solutions engineering engagements where the customer requests Dedicated capacity with autoscaling and must maintain compliance constraints (no public spot by default).

Key goals:
- Keep committed baseline (predictable spend) for critical traffic.
- Allow controlled burst capacity for marketing spikes or demo days with cost caps.
- Ensure graceful degradation when capacity or budget is exhausted rather than hard failures.
- Provide clear cost model for committed + burst usage and an experiment plan to validate assumptions.

Customer scenario example (fictional):
- Customer: mid-market SaaS with document summarization feature integrated across product; peak demo traffic during release cycles.
- Target SLO: p95 latency <= 350ms for 512-token responses for interactive users.
- Typical steady QPS: 60 requests/sec (avg 120 tokens per response).
- Burst scenario: occasional 5–20 minute peaks up to 300 requests/sec.
- Compliance: private data, Dedicated pool required, spot/ephemeral GPUs restricted to non-customer-data tasks.

Sizing recommendation (baseline + burst):
1) Baseline pool (committed): pick GPU flavor that meets p95 under typical load with margin. For this customer, H100-equivalent gives ~600 tokens/sec throughput per GPU for our tuned Llama-style quantized model at batch= auto.
   - Baseline capacity target = sustain 60 qps * 120 tokens = 7,200 tokens/sec required.
   - GPUs needed = ceil(7,200 / 600) = 12 GPUs (committed).
   - This meets latency headroom for autoscaling and avoids cold-starts.

2) Burst overlay (on-demand reserved or short-term reserved nodes):
   - Bursting target = additional capacity to reach 300 qps -> incremental tokens/sec = (300-60)*120 = 28,800 tokens/sec.
   - Additional GPUs = ceil(28,800 / 600) = 48 GPUs for peak burst.
   - Practically, recommend staged burst pools: small fast scale (16 GPUs) + larger cheaper burst (up to 48 GPUs) with admission control (see policy below).

Autoscaling policy (recommended):
- Multi-tier pools: baseline committed pool (12 GPUs), rapid-burst pool (16 GPUs, fast provisioning from warm standby images), and elastic-burst pool (up to 48 GPUs, lower-priority warm VMs that take ~90–180s to ramp).
- Scale triggers: short-window p95 latency > target AND queue depth > threshold -> trigger rapid-burst; if short-window sustained > 60–90s, add elastic-burst.
- Cooldown: 120s for rapid-burst downscale, 600s for elastic-burst downscale to avoid oscillation.
- Warm standby: maintain a small set of pre-warmed nodes (1–2 GPUs worth of capacity) in elastic-burst so first allocation is quicker without violating compliance controls.
- Admission control and backpressure: when all pools saturated, apply graceful degradation (see below) rather than returning 503s.

Graceful degradation strategy (user-facing priorities):
1) Response shaping: reduce max tokens or use a faster, smaller model variant for non-critical routes (configured per-route). Example: truncate to 256 tokens or switch to a 7B quantized variant for low-priority requests.
2) Priority queueing: tag requests (interactive vs batch) and only serve interactive at baseline; batch jobs are delayed or redirected to offline processing.
3) Probabilistic sampling: serve deterministic fraction of low-priority requests (e.g., 50%) during sustained overload.
4) Fallback models: pre-uploaded lightweight model in Dedicated pool (half throughput cost, lower latency predictability) used automatically when primary model capacity exhausted.
5) Soft-fail responses: return cached summaries for repeated doc IDs where available.

Cost estimate framework (example monthly):
- Baseline 12 H100-equivalent GPUs at committed rate: assume $15k/GPU/month (this is an illustrative placeholder; replace with current pricing from infra sales).
   - Baseline cost = 12 * $15,000 = $180,000/month.
- Rapid-burst 16 GPUs on short-term reserved (premium) when used: assume $18k/GPU-month pro-rated by usage. If used 2 hours/day average -> pro-rate factor = (2/24) = 0.083 -> monthly cost = 16 * $18,000 * 0.083 ≈ $23,904.
- Elastic-burst up to 48 GPUs at lower-priority rate (e.g., $11k/GPU-month pro-rated). If used 1 hour/week average -> pro-rate factor ≈ (1/168) = 0.006 -> cost = 48 * $11,000 * 0.006 ≈ $3,168.
- Total illustrative monthly = $180,000 + $23,904 + $3,168 = $207,072.
- Unit economics: convert to per-request token cost by measuring actual token/sec efficiency in POC. Example: at baseline throughput delivering 60 qps * 120 tokens * 3600s * 24 * 30 = ~622M tokens/month; cost/token ≈ $0.33 per million tokens. (Use benchmark runs in the lab to produce actual throughput and adjust.)

Tradeoffs and operational notes:
- Committing to many GPUs reduces per-token unit cost but increases fixed monthly spend. For customers sensitive to spend, recommend a lower committed baseline + a defined monthly burst budget and strict admission control.
- Warm image maintenance: keep model weights on local NVMe to avoid cold-pull time; image patching and drift schedule must be part of ops checklist.
- Telemetry: ensure per-request model version, GPU id, queue time, and latency buckets emitted. Tie alerts to cost-runbooks (e.g., if burst spend exceeds configured budget, trigger an ops-runbook and temporary throttling policy).

Workshop experiment plan (3-step POC):
1) Lab validation (week 0–1): benchmark model throughput (tokens/sec) on the target GPU flavor with typical prompts; measure p50/p95 at batch sizes matching production distribution.
2) Controlled stress test (week 2): synthetic traffic to reproduce burst profiles; validate autoscaler trigger timings, warm-standby ramp, and graceful-degradation behavior. Capture metrics and adjust thresholds.
3) Production pilot (week 3–6): run with a small subset of real traffic in dedicated pool, monitor cost delta, user-visible latency, and fallback incidence. Finalize committed counts and SLA language.

Runbook snippets (quick):
- If p95 exceeds target for >120s -> enable rapid-burst pool and notify SE on-call.
- If burst spend forecasted to exceed monthly cap -> reduce elastic-burst max to 25% and switch low-priority requests to fallback model.
- If warm image corruption detected on startup -> route new requests to fallback model and roll image across baseline nodes.

Open questions to take to customer workshop:
- Acceptable monthly committed spend range? (anchor first: $150–250k/mo example above)
- Policy on spot-like GPUs for non-customer-data workloads (can we use cheaper spot instances for batch/offline jobs?).
- Priority mapping: which routes are interactive vs batch; do we have clear per-route SLAs to implement admission control?

Next steps before customer workshop:
- Run benchmark scripts on H100 and A100-equivalent nodes to validate tokens/sec numbers (owner: Ethan Cole, due 2024-09-22).
- Create autoscaler simulation harness to replay historical traffic (owner: Marina Velasquez, due 2024-09-29).
- Draft customer-facing one-pager with cost bands and degradation UX examples (owner: Priya Raman, due 2024-10-02).

Notes: this doc is deliberately prescriptive and conservative for POC acceptance. Replace placeholder price points with procurement quotes during scoping. Keep degradation UX options flexible and capture customer tolerance during the workshop.

End of working note.
